option_description: Whether untrusted input is validated server-side against an allow-list (what IS permitted) — syntactic (anchored regex, length, charset) plus semantic (business-range) — at the trust boundary, rather than via a bypassable deny-list or client-side-only checks.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "Missing server-side allow-list input validation" — this is the primary attribute that rule keys on: when server_side_allowlist_validation is true, untrusted input is constrained at the trust boundary, mitigating the A03 injection family (T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application) as a contributing control behind parameterization and output encoding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review each input field's validation rule for an allow-list (fixed-set match or anchored regex with bounded length and explicit charset). Confirm deny-list-only or client-side-only validation is not relied upon.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each input field maps to an allow-list rule (fixed set match, or anchored ^...$ regex with min/max length and explicit charset). Deny-list-only filtering or client-side-only validation is INSECURE — JS validation is circumvented by disabling JS or using a proxy.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm validation runs server-side before any processing, as early as data is received, and includes both syntactic and semantic checks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Validation runs server-side before any data is processed, as early as the data is received. Both syntactic (format) and semantic (business-context, e.g. start-date < end-date, value-in-range) checks present.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether the only input validation present is in client-side JavaScript (no server-side enforcement) — a security-worthless posture, since client checks are bypassed by disabling JS or using an intercepting proxy.
security_impact: An OR-trigger for "Missing server-side allow-list input validation" — this is the inverse of the protection: when validation_is_client_side_only is true, no server-side guard exists, leaving the trust boundary undefended against the A03 injection family (T1190). The control is present only when this is false (validation also runs server-side).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Determine whether validation logic exists only in front-end JavaScript by checking that the same rules are re-enforced server-side before processing.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Validation runs server-side before any data is processed, as early as the data is received. Both syntactic (format) and semantic (business-context, e.g. start-date < end-date, value-in-range) checks present.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet

how_to_obtain.instruction: Submit a malformed value via an intercepting proxy (e.g. Burp/ZAP), bypassing the browser, and observe whether the server rejects it.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A proxied request carrying values that the client-side JS would reject is still rejected by the server. If the server accepts it, validation was client-side-only and is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: general-knowledge

option_description: Whether input handling relies on a deny-list/blacklist of bad characters or patterns rather than an allow-list of what is permitted — a bypass-prone approach (encoding, alternate representations, and novel payloads evade fixed deny-lists).
security_impact: An OR-trigger for "Missing server-side allow-list input validation" — deny-list filtering is the insecure substitute for the allow-list control: when denylist_filtering_used is true, the boundary is bypassable, contributing to the A03 injection family (T1190). The control is satisfied only when validation is allow-list-based, not deny-list-based.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect validation routines to determine whether they reject known-bad patterns (deny-list) versus matching against a permitted set (allow-list).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each input field maps to an allow-list rule (fixed set match, or anchored ^...$ regex with min/max length and explicit charset). Deny-list-only filtering or client-side-only validation is INSECURE — JS validation is circumvented by disabling JS or using a proxy.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether all database access uses parameterized queries / prepared statements (placeholders bind user input as data) rather than string-concatenated SQL — the primary SQL-injection defense.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "SQL / NoSQL / LDAP injection" — this is the primary attribute that rule keys on: when parameterized_queries_used is true, the interpreter separates code from data, mitigating SQL/NoSQL/LDAP injection (T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application). The exposure fires when this protection is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep the source for SQL built by concatenating user input; confirm queries use placeholders bound separately via prepared statements.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No SQL string built by concatenating user input. Secure code passes a placeholder query (? or named params) to prepareStatement/PreparedStatement and binds values separately. Concatenation into the query string is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether user input is concatenated into the SQL/query string ("... WHERE name = " + input) or escaping is relied on as the primary defense — the canonical SQL-injection root cause.
security_impact: An OR-trigger for "SQL / NoSQL / LDAP injection" — this is the insecure inverse of parameterization: when dynamic_query_string_concatenation is true, attacker input alters query structure, contributing to SQL/NoSQL/LDAP injection (T1190). The injection exposure fires when this is true; the control is present only when it is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep the source for concatenation of user input into query strings; any match indicates dynamic query-string concatenation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No SQL string built by concatenating user input. Secure code passes a placeholder query (? or named params) to prepareStatement/PreparedStatement and binds values separately. Concatenation into the query string is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether the database account used by the application runs at least privilege (no DBA/admin rights, only the required SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE) — bounding the blast radius if SQL injection succeeds.
security_impact: Protection that contributes to the countermeasure for "SQL / NoSQL / LDAP injection" — when least_privilege_db_account is true, a successful injection has a limited blast radius; it is a defense-in-depth attribute behind parameterized_queries_used for the same exposure (T1190).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the database grants for the application's service account to confirm it lacks DBA/admin rights and holds only the privileges the app requires.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DB account used by the app has least privilege (no DBA/admin, only required SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE), limiting blast radius if SQLi succeeds.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether all untrusted data rendered into a response is encoded for its exact output context (HTML body, attribute, JS, CSS, URL) — typically via framework auto-escaping, with escape-hatches avoided — the primary XSS defense.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "Cross-site scripting (reflected / stored / DOM)" — this is the primary attribute that rule keys on: when contextual_output_encoding_applied is true, untrusted data cannot break out of its render context into script (CWE-79, T1059.007). The XSS exposure fires when this protection is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep for unsafe DOM sinks and framework escape-hatches; confirm untrusted data instead flows through context-matched encoding or a safe sink.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Untrusted data flows through context-matched encoding or a safe sink (.textContent, createTextNode). Unsafe sinks (innerHTML/outerHTML/eval) with untrusted data are INSECURE unless wrapped in DOMPurify.sanitize().
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Cross-Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm rich/user-authored HTML is sanitised with DOMPurify before rendering rather than hand-encoded.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rich/user-authored HTML is sanitised with DOMPurify before rendering, not hand-encoded.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Cross-Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether untrusted data reaches unsafe sinks (innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write, eval, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, bypassSecurityTrustAs*) without sanitisation — the DOM-XSS root cause.
security_impact: An OR-trigger for "Cross-site scripting (reflected / stored / DOM)" — this is the insecure inverse of contextual encoding: when unsafe_html_sinks_used is true (and data is not DOMPurify-sanitised), script can be injected into the victim browser (CWE-79, T1059.007). The XSS exposure fires when this is true; the control is present only when safe sinks/sanitisation are used.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep for unsafe HTML/JS sinks; any match on untrusted data not wrapped in DOMPurify.sanitize() indicates an unsafe sink.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Untrusted data flows through context-matched encoding or a safe sink (.textContent, createTextNode). Unsafe sinks (innerHTML/outerHTML/eval) with untrusted data are INSECURE unless wrapped in DOMPurify.sanitize().
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Cross-Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether a per-application Content-Security-Policy response header is set, restricting script sources / inline script as XSS defense-in-depth — layered behind output encoding, never the sole defense.
security_impact: Protection that contributes to the countermeasure for "Cross-site scripting (reflected / stored / DOM)" — when content_security_policy_enforced is true, a tuned CSP provides defense-in-depth that limits script execution even if encoding is bypassed (CWE-79, T1059.007). It is a layered control behind contextual_output_encoding_applied for the same exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the application and inspect response headers for a scoped Content-Security-Policy.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A Content-Security-Policy header is returned and scoped to the app. CSP is defense-in-depth — its absence is a gap; relying on it alone is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Secure Headers Project (CSP for XSS defense-in-depth)

option_description: Whether user input is concatenated into a single shell command string (system(), shell=True, Runtime.exec with one string, escapeshellcmd as the guard) — the OS command-injection root cause.
security_impact: An OR-trigger for "OS command injection" — this is the insecure inverse of safe process invocation: when user_input_in_shell_command_string is true, attacker input executes arbitrary OS commands (CWE-78, T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter). The command-injection exposure fires when this is true; the control is present only when it is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep for shell-string process invocation; any match passing user input indicates input reaching a shell string.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No user input reaches a shell string. Secure: native library call, or argument-array spawn with each arg a separate element. Single concatenated command string or shell=True with user data is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether OS-level operations use built-in library functions, or — when a process must spawn — argument-array invocation (separate args, no shell), an allow-listed command, validated args, and the -- option-terminator — the OS command-injection defense.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "OS command injection" — when os_commands_avoided_or_arg_array_used is true, user data never becomes part of a shell string, mitigating OS command injection (CWE-78, T1059). The exposure fires when this protection is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep for process-spawn calls and confirm they use native library functions or argument-array form with each arg a separate element rather than a concatenated command string.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No user input reaches a shell string. Secure: native library call, or argument-array spawn with each arg a separate element. Single concatenated command string or shell=True with user data is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether the application natively/binary-deserializes untrusted data (Java ObjectInputStream.readObject/XMLDecoder, Python pickle.load/yaml.load, PHP unserialize, .NET BinaryFormatter or TypeNameHandling != None) — the insecure-deserialization RCE root cause.
security_impact: An OR-trigger for "Insecure deserialization of untrusted data" — this is the insecure inverse of the deserialization control: when native_deserialization_of_untrusted_data is true, gadget chains can reach remote code execution (T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application). The exposure fires when this is true; the control is present only when pure-data formats or signed/allow-listed deserialization are used.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep for native deserialization sinks; any match on attacker-controlled data indicates native deserialization of untrusted data.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No native deserialization of untrusted data. Secure: JSON/XML parsing, yaml.safe_load, TypeNameHandling.None, ObjectInputStream with resolveClass allow-list. Any of the listed sinks on attacker-controlled data is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Deserialization Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether, where native serialization is unavoidable, deserialization is constrained by a class allow-list (resolveClass / serialization filter) and/or serialized blobs are signed (HMAC) and verified before deserialization, with hardcoded types.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "Insecure deserialization of untrusted data" — when deserialization_class_allowlist_or_signed_payloads is true, gadget chains and tampered blobs are rejected before deserialization, mitigating deserialization RCE (T1190). It is the present-protection complement to native_deserialization_of_untrusted_data for that exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm that where native serialization is required, the blob is signed (HMAC/digital signature) and verified before deserialization and that class types are hardcoded, not user-controlled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Where native serialization is required, the blob is signed (HMAC/digital signature) and the signature is verified before deserialization; class types are hardcoded, not user-controlled.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Deserialization Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether XML parsers disable DTDs / external entities (ideally DOCTYPE entirely): Java disallow-doctype-decl=true + FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, .NET DtdProcessing.Prohibit / XmlResolver=null, Python defusedxml — preventing XXE file disclosure/SSRF.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "XXE and entity-expansion DoS" — this is the primary attribute that rule keys on: when xml_external_entities_disabled is true, the parser will not resolve external entities, mitigating XXE file disclosure/SSRF (T1190). The exposure fires when this protection is absent — many parsers (notably Java JAXP) enable XXE by default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep for XML parser hardening directives; confirm parsers fed untrusted XML explicitly disable DOCTYPE/external entities.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Parser explicitly disables DOCTYPE/external entities (Java setFeature disallow-doctype-decl=true; .NET DtdProcessing.Prohibit; defusedxml in Python). Absence of hardening on a parser fed untrusted XML is INSECURE — many parsers enable XXE by default.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP XML External Entity Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether XML parsing enforces entity-expansion limits (and ideally disallows DOCTYPE) — preventing billion-laughs / nested entity-expansion denial of service.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "XXE and entity-expansion DoS" — when entity_expansion_limits_enforced is true, nested entity expansion cannot exhaust memory/CPU, mitigating the billion-laughs DoS facet of that exposure (T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service). It is the DoS-facet complement to xml_external_entities_disabled for the same exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm the XML parser disallows DOCTYPE or enforces secure-processing / entity-expansion limits (e.g. defusedxml in Python, FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING in Java) on untrusted XML.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Parser explicitly disables DOCTYPE/external entities (Java setFeature disallow-doctype-decl=true; .NET DtdProcessing.Prohibit; defusedxml in Python). Absence of hardening on a parser fed untrusted XML is INSECURE — many parsers enable XXE by default.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP XML External Entity Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether user-controlled file paths/names are canonicalised and confined to an allow-listed base directory (server-defined paths, random/UUID names) — preventing path traversal / local file inclusion.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the path-traversal facet of the countermeasure for "Path traversal and SSRF from un-allow-listed destinations" — when file_paths_canonicalized_and_contained is true, ../ traversal cannot escape the intended base directory (CWE-73, T1083 File and Directory Discovery). That exposure's path-traversal trigger fires when this protection is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm file paths are server-defined and that user text is never used as a path component without canonicalisation plus a base-directory containment check.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File paths are server-defined; user text is never used as a path component without canonicalisation + base-directory containment check. Direct use of user filename in a path is INSECURE (maps to CWE-73).
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether server-side outbound requests built from user-supplied URLs/hosts are constrained by an allow-list of permitted schemes/hosts/ports, with HTTP redirects disabled or re-validated — preventing SSRF.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the SSRF facet of the countermeasure for "Path traversal and SSRF from un-allow-listed destinations" — this is the primary SSRF attribute that rule keys on: when outbound_fetch_destination_allowlisted is true, the server only fetches trusted destinations, mitigating SSRF (T1090 Proxy). That exposure's SSRF trigger fires when raw user URLs are fetched (this protection absent).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review outbound-fetch code to confirm the target host is validated against an allow-list of trusted hosts/schemes and that redirects are disabled or re-validated.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Outbound-fetch code validates the target host against an allow-list and rejects private/link-local/metadata ranges (169.254.169.254 included); redirects disabled or re-validated. Fetching a raw user URL is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether private (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, ::1), link-local, and cloud-metadata (169.254.169.254, metadata.amazonaws.com) targets are rejected for outbound fetches, with network-layer egress restrictions as defense-in-depth.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the SSRF facet of the countermeasure for "Path traversal and SSRF from un-allow-listed destinations" — when private_and_metadata_targets_blocked is true, an attacker cannot pivot an outbound fetch to internal services or cloud metadata (T1090 Proxy). It is the internal-range complement to outbound_fetch_destination_allowlisted for that exposure's SSRF facet.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm outbound-fetch code rejects private/link-local/metadata ranges (including 169.254.169.254) and parses IPs with a vetted library.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Outbound-fetch code validates the target host against an allow-list and rejects private/link-local/metadata ranges (169.254.169.254 included); redirects disabled or re-validated. Fetching a raw user URL is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm network-layer egress restrictions (firewall/segmentation) limit outbound traffic to legitimate destinations as defense-in-depth, independent of the app-layer allow-list.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Network-layer egress restrictions (firewall/segmentation) limit outbound traffic to legitimate destinations as defense-in-depth, independent of the app-layer allow-list.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether uploaded files are validated by an extension allow-list AND file-signature/magic-byte inspection of actual content (not trusting the client Content-Type) — a primary defense against web-shell upload.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "Unrestricted file upload (web shell)" — this is the primary attribute that rule keys on: when upload_extension_allowlist_and_magic_byte_validation is true, disguised executables (.jpg.php, content-type spoofing) are rejected, mitigating web-shell upload (T1505.003 Server Software Component: Web Shell). The exposure fires when this protection is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep the upload handler and confirm it checks an extension allow-list AND validates file signature/magic bytes from actual content, ignoring/validating the client Content-Type.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Upload handler checks an extension allow-list AND file signature/magic bytes, ignores/validates client Content-Type, renames to a random name (UUID), and writes outside the webroot to a non-executable dir. Trusting client Content-Type or using the user filename is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether uploaded files are stored outside the webroot in a non-executable directory — so an uploaded file cannot be requested and executed as code.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "Unrestricted file upload (web shell)" — when uploads_stored_nonexecutable_outside_webroot is true, even an uploaded executable cannot be served and run, mitigating web-shell execution (T1505.003). It is the storage-location complement to upload_extension_allowlist_and_magic_byte_validation for that exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm the upload handler writes files outside the webroot to a non-executable directory rather than into an executable webroot path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Upload handler checks an extension allow-list AND file signature/magic bytes, ignores/validates client Content-Type, renames to a random name (UUID), and writes outside the webroot to a non-executable dir. Trusting client Content-Type or using the user filename is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether uploaded files are renamed to a random/server-defined name (e.g. UUID) rather than retaining the user-supplied filename — defeating filename-based path/extension tricks and overwrite attacks.
security_impact: Protection that contributes to the countermeasure for "Unrestricted file upload (web shell)" — when uploads_randomly_renamed is true, the user-supplied filename never drives storage path or extension, mitigating filename-based web-shell tricks (T1505.003). It is a defense-in-depth attribute behind upload_extension_allowlist_and_magic_byte_validation for that exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm the upload handler renames files to a random name (e.g. UUID) and never uses the user-supplied filename as the stored name or path.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Upload handler checks an extension allow-list AND file signature/magic bytes, ignores/validates client Content-Type, renames to a random name (UUID), and writes outside the webroot to a non-executable dir. Trusting client Content-Type or using the user filename is INSECURE.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether maximum request/field/upload sizes are enforced before processing and ZIP target path/level/estimated-unzip-size are validated pre-extraction — preventing oversized-payload DoS and decompression bombs.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "Oversized/complex-payload DoS and mass assignment" — this is the primary attribute that rule keys on: when request_size_and_complexity_limits_enforced is true, unbounded bodies/fields/uploads and decompression bombs cannot exhaust resources, mitigating the DoS facet (T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service). That exposure's DoS trigger fires when this protection is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm a maximum file/request size is enforced before processing and that ZIP entries are validated for target path, compression level, and estimated unzip size before extraction.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A maximum file/request size is enforced before processing; ZIP entries validated for target path, compression level and estimated unzip size before extraction.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether validation regexes are anchored (^...$), use bounded length quantifiers (e.g. {1,25}), and avoid catastrophic-backtracking wildcards (. / \S over user input) — mitigating ReDoS.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the countermeasure for "Oversized/complex-payload DoS and mass assignment" — when redos_safe_regexes is true, catastrophic-backtracking cannot exhaust CPU, mitigating the ReDoS facet of that exposure (T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service). It is the regex-complexity complement to request_size_and_complexity_limits_enforced for the DoS facet.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review validation regexes to confirm they are anchored, use bounded length quantifiers, and avoid 'any character' wildcards like . or \S that enable catastrophic backtracking.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Validation regexes are anchored (^...$), use bounded length quantifiers (e.g. {1,25}) and avoid 'any character' wildcards like . or \S, mitigating ReDoS.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet

option_description: Whether request-to-object binding is restricted to an allow-list of bindable fields (Spring setAllowedFields, Rails strong params, .NET [Bind]) or routed through a DTO/view-model that omits sensitive fields — preventing mass assignment / over-posting.
security_impact: Protection that satisfies the mass-assignment facet of the countermeasure for "Oversized/complex-payload DoS and mass assignment" — when bindable_field_allowlist_enforced is true, attackers cannot over-post sensitive fields (e.g. &isAdmin=true) for privilege escalation (T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application). That exposure's mass-assignment trigger fires when request params auto-bind to a domain entity with no allow-list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep controllers for a bindable-field allow-list or DTO binding; confirm request params are not auto-bound straight onto domain entities with sensitive fields.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Controllers either bind to a DTO (sensitive fields absent) or declare an allow-list of bindable fields. Binding request params straight onto a domain entity with no allow-list is INSECURE — enables privilege-escalation over-posting.
how_to_obtain.source: OWASP Mass Assignment Cheat Sheet
